newsitem.title: CHINA: China unlikely to support stocks during HK handover.
newsitem.headline: China unlikely to support stocks during HK handover.

text.p: Beijing is unlikely to take measures to support the stock markets in China and Hong Kong up to and during the Chinese takeover of the British colony, barring major problems, stock analysts said on Friday.

The stability of the markets in the aftermath of the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping has prompted widespread speculation that the authorities have been intervening in some way or another to support prices.

"I believe it is unnecessary for the central government to support the markets even though it badly wants the markets to be stable in this year of Hong Kong's return," said an executive with a major Chinese brokerage.
"The stability seen after Deng's death on the mainland and Hong Kong's stock markets has indicated that there will be no sharp flucations unless something unforseeable happens," he added.

"I don't see that there's really any need to (prop up the markets)," said Alex Conroy, an analyst in Shanghai with ING-Barings. "I can see they would want stability in the initial week after Deng's death, but apart from that, people don't seem too concerned about political instability."

Rumours have also been circulating that Chinese money is entering the Hong Kong market to help keep stock prices on an upward trend towards the Chinese take-over of the colony at midnight on June 30, stock analysts said.

"There have been a lot of rumours that quasi-official Chinese entities in Hong Kong are buying, but I don't see any reason for it at this point," Conroy said. "If they are buying, it is probably just because they see a chance to make some money."

Stock prices on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges have risen solidly since the death of Deng, and analysts said investors have confidence in China's continued stability and short-term market trends.
Deng died late on the night of February 19, but his death was not announced until the next day.
"It looks very much like government-related institutions stepped in to support share prices the day Beijing announced the death of Deng Xiaoping," said an analyst with a Shenzhen brokerage.
"But it's only my guess, it is impossible to get evidence," he said. "Huge amounts of buying orders suddenly arrived for some index-weighted counters, seconds after that day's opening.

"Usually, institutions would stay on the sidelines or trim holdings when major bad news comes out. Many brokers had previously expected all (China's) A-share prices to close at their 10 percent limit-down levels that day," he added.
"I felt there was an 'invisible hand' in the market that day," said another broker.
The central authorities, in a major message to the markets in mid-December, warned that the government would not step in to help investors in the event of a major market crash.
Some analysts said it looked more likely the authorities would intervene to prevent rises in prices rather than falls.

"The authorities are more concerned about surges than plunges on the markets, judging from recent developments," said a domestic A-share dealer. "They are more likely to instruct brokerages to refrain from speculation than to ask them to support the markets."
